docs.title: Home
docs.text: The H₂O–NaCl system at 250 bar, about the pressure at the seafloor at 2.5 km water depth. Shaded regions are where the fluid splits into two phases: vapour + liquid (pink), vapour + halite (grey) and liquid + halite (light blue). Elsewhere the fluid is a single phase, coloured by its density, which drops sharply between 380 and 400 °C. Seawater (dashed line) starts to separate into a vapour and a brine at about 388 °C. The phase-region geometry comes from Slice_constP, the densities from xthermo.tpx.

docs.title: xThermo
docs.text:
Phase relations and thermodynamic properties of H₂O–NaCl fluids from 0 to 1000 °C and 1 to 5000 bar, after Driesner & Heinrich (2007) and Driesner (2007). A C++ library for simulation codes, with a Python interface for NumPy and Matplotlib.

Get started Gallery Model and limitations

docs.title: What xThermo computes
docs.text:
• Phase relations

    Liquid, vapour and halite, their two- and three-phase coexistence and the critical curve of the binary, as functions of temperature, pressure and salinity.

  • Fluid properties

    Density, specific enthalpy, heat capacity, viscosity and density derivatives of each phase and of the mixture, from T–p–X or H–p–X (enthalpy-based) input.

  • Python for science

    xthermo.tpx and xthermo.hpx evaluate whole NumPy grids, with an explicit error policy, and plotting helpers draw phase diagrams and property maps.

  • C++ for simulation codes

    A CMake package (find_package(xThermo)), exceptions or non-throwing evaluation with status codes, and one model instance per thread or MPI rank.

  • Pure water and NaCl

    Water from IAPS-84 (the basis of the Driesner model) or IAPWS-95; pure NaCl solid, liquid and vapour.

  • Checked against the literature

    Compared with the published tables of the Driesner papers and the IAPWS releases. Known differences and limitations are documented: Model and limitations.

docs.title: Seawater, heated at 250 bar
docs.text:
Following the dashed line of the figure above. Below about 388 °C seawater is a single liquid. Between 388 and 449 °C it splits into a vapour of low salinity and an increasingly saline brine; the vapour soon carries most of the mass. Above about 449 °C the brine is gone, and halite coexists with a vapour whose salinity keeps falling. This is the kind of phase separation seen in hydrothermal systems at mid-ocean ridges. Python code for both figures 
"""Homepage figures: the H2O-NaCl phase diagram at 250 bar with the density of the single-phase fluid, and seawater
heated at 250 bar.

Writes hero_desktop.png, hero_mobile.png and seawater_250bar.png to docs/assets/img (or the directory given as the
first argument or in $XTHERMO_FIGURE_DIR). Needs xthermo and matplotlib.
"""
import os

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

import _style as st

st.apply()
OUT = st.outdir(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), "..", "assets", "img"))

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
P = 250e5                      # Pa
X_SEAWATER = 0.032             # kg/kg (3.2 wt% NaCl)

# fluid density on a T-X grid; the multiphase regions are drawn over it by plot_slice
T = np.linspace(1, 999, 400) + 273.15
X = np.logspace(-5, 0, 400)
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, T[:, None], P, X[None, :], errors="nan")
section = sw.Slice_constP(P)

# seawater heated at 250 bar: where it separates into brine and vapour, and how salty each phase is
Tp = np.linspace(300, 600, 601) + 273.15
q = xthermo.tpx(sw, Tp, P, X_SEAWATER, errors="nan")
two_phase = q.has("vapour") & q.has("liquid")
vapour_mass = np.where(q.ok, q.S_v * q.Rho_v / q.Rho, np.nan)
tc = Tp - 273.15
T_SPLIT = tc[two_phase].min()       # °C, where seawater starts to separate into vapour and brine
T_HALITE = tc[two_phase].max()      # °C, above it vapour + halite


def phase_diagram(figsize, fontsize, labels, note, note_xy):
    with plt.rc_context({"font.size": fontsize}):
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
        ax.set_xscale("log")
        field = xthermo.plot_property(ax, s, "Rho", x="X", y="T", cmap=st.OCEAN, vmin=0, vmax=1300, colorbar=False)
        xthermo.plot_slice(ax, section, x="X", y="T", points=False)
        ax.axvline(X_SEAWATER * 100, color=st.CORAL, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (5, 3)), zorder=5)
        ax.set_xlim(1e-3, 100)
        ax.set_ylim(0, 1000)
        ax.set_xlabel("bulk salinity (wt% NaCl)")
        ax.set_ylabel("temperature (°C)")
        cb = fig.colorbar(field["mesh"], ax=ax, pad=0.015, fraction=0.04, aspect=30)
        cb.set_label("density of the single-phase fluid (kg/m³)")
        cb.outline.set_visible(False)
        for x, y, text, colour in labels:
            ax.text(x, y, text, color=colour, ha="center", va="center", zorder=6)
        ax.text(X_SEAWATER * 100 * 1.12, 965, "seawater", color=st.CORAL, ha="left", va="top", zorder=6,
                fontweight="bold")
        ax.plot([X_SEAWATER * 100], [T_SPLIT], "o", ms=fontsize * 0.7, mfc=st.CORAL, mec="white", mew=1.5, zorder=7)
        ax.annotate(note, (X_SEAWATER * 100, T_SPLIT), xytext=note_xy, color="white", ha="right", va="center",
                    zorder=7, fontsize=fontsize * 0.9, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color="white", lw=1))
        ax.set_title("H₂O–NaCl at 250 bar")
    return fig


desktop = phase_diagram((11, 5.2), 11, [
    (1.0, 870, "vapour + liquid", st.NAVY),
    (3, 600, "vapour + halite", st.INK),
    (68, 120, "liquid\n+ halite", st.NAVY),
    (5e-3, 110, "liquid-like fluid", "white"),
    (5e-3, 620, "vapour-like fluid", st.INK),
], f"seawater separates into\nvapour + brine at ≈{T_SPLIT:.0f} °C", (0.9, 250))
desktop.text(0.0, -0.02, st.CREDIT, fontsize=8, color=st.MUTED, transform=desktop.transFigure)
desktop.savefig(os.path.join(OUT, "hero_desktop.png"))

mobile = phase_diagram((6.2, 6.4), 14, [
    (1.0, 870, "V + L", st.NAVY),
    (3, 600, "V + H", st.INK),
    (52, 110, "L+H", st.NAVY),
    (6e-3, 120, "liquid-like", "white"),
], f"splits at\n≈{T_SPLIT:.0f} °C", (0.9, 260))
mobile.savefig(os.path.join(OUT, "hero_mobile.png"))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.0))
ax.axvspan(T_SPLIT, T_HALITE, color="#ddeef3", lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.axvspan(T_HALITE, tc[-1], color="#eeeeee", lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.semilogy(tc, np.where(q.has("liquid"), q.X_l * 100, np.nan), color=st.NAVY, lw=2.2, label="liquid (brine)")
ax.semilogy(tc, np.where(q.has("vapour"), q.X_v * 100, np.nan), color=st.CORAL, lw=2.2, label="vapour")
ax.set_ylabel("salinity of the phase (wt% NaCl)")
ax.set_xlabel("temperature (°C)")
ax.set_xlim(tc[0], tc[-1])
ax.legend(loc="upper right", bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.86))
ax2 = ax.twinx()
ax2.spines["right"].set_visible(True)
ax2.plot(tc, vapour_mass * 100, color=st.TEAL, lw=1.4, ls="--")
ax2.set_ylim(0, 100)
ax2.set_ylabel("vapour mass fraction (%)", color=st.TEAL)
ax2.tick_params(axis="y", colors=st.TEAL)
ax.text((T_SPLIT + T_HALITE) / 2, 0.25, "vapour\n+ brine", ha="center", va="center", color=st.INK)
ax.text((T_HALITE + tc[-1]) / 2, 0.25, "vapour + halite", ha="center", va="center", color=st.INK)
ax.text((tc[0] + T_SPLIT) / 2, 0.25, "liquid", ha="center", va="center", color=st.INK)
ax.set_title("Seawater (3.2 wt% NaCl) heated at 250 bar")
fig.text(0.0, -0.03, st.CREDIT, fontsize=7.5, color=st.MUTED, transform=fig.transFigure)
fig.savefig(os.path.join(OUT, "seawater_250bar.png"))
print("hero_desktop.png hero_mobile.png seawater_250bar.png written to", os.path.abspath(OUT))

The script uses a few shared style settings from docs/gallery/_style.py.

Authors
docs.text:
xThermo is developed at the GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel.

Zhikui Guo: original developer. He wrote the C++ library, the water and NaCl backends and the Python bindings, building on earlier GEOMAR MATLAB implementations of the Driesner model.

Lars Rüpke: scientific maintainer and project lead.

xThermo is used in hydrothermal-system modelling at GEOMAR, for example in the OpenFOAM-based solvers of HydrothermalFoam.

docs.title: How to cite
docs.text:
The equation of state implemented in xThermo is the work of Thomas Driesner and Christoph Heinrich. Please cite the two papers when you use xThermo:

Driesner, T. & Heinrich, C.A. (2007). The system H₂O–NaCl. Part I: Correlation formulae for phase relations in temperature–pressure–composition space from 0 to 1000 °C, 0 to 5000 bar, and 0 to 1 XNaCl. Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, 71, 4880–4901. doi:10.1016/j.gca.2006.01.033

Driesner, T. (2007). The system H₂O–NaCl. Part II: Correlations for molar volume, enthalpy, and isobaric heat capacity from 0 to 1000 °C, 1 to 5000 bar, and 0 to 1 XNaCl. Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta, 71, 4902–4919. doi:10.1016/j.gca.2007.05.026

For the water properties, cite the formulation you use: IAPS-84 (Haar, Gallagher & Kell 1984, NBS/NRC Steam Tables, Hemisphere, Washington) or IAPWS-95 (Wagner & Pruß 2002, J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data 31, 387–535).

To refer to the software itself, cite it as xThermo, GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel, https://github.com/lruepke/xThermo, with the version you used (xthermo.__version__). A citable DOI for xThermo is planned.

docs.title: Command-line tool
docs.text:
xThermal evaluates the models from the shell: single states, profiles, grids and files of points. It is installed with the library in <prefix>/bin/. Every example on this page runs in the documentation's test suite exactly as printed.

xThermal <program> [options]
xThermal <program> -h          help for one program
xThermal -h | -v               general help, version
Program Purpose thermo evaluate states from T–p–X or H–p–X input lutgen, lutinfo, lookup, lut2vtu build, inspect, query and convert adaptive lookup tables (below)

docs.title: A first example
docs.text:
Seawater-like brine (10 wt% NaCl) at 300 °C and 300 bar:

xThermal thermo -D0 -VPTX -T300 -P300E5 -X0.1

H2O-NaCl
T=300 deg.C = 573.15 K, P=300 bar, X=10 wt% NaCl, H=1.21693e+06 J/kg
  phase: Liquid
  Rho=849.034 [kg/m^3]
  H=1.21693e+06 [J/kg]
  Cp=4407.72 [J/kg/K]
  Mu=0.000114076 [Pa S]
  dRhodT=-1.3541 [kg/m3/K]
  dRhodP=1.06661e-06 [kg/m3/Pa]
  Isothermal compressibility=1.25627e-09 [1/Pa]
  Isobaric expansivity=0.00159487 [1/K]

The values are those of the Python and C++ interfaces (xthermo.tpx(sw, 573.15, 300e5, 0.1)).

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
Temperature: °C on the command line, K in files

-T and the temperature ranges of -R are in degrees Celsius. Input files (-G) and every output file (CSV and VTK) use kelvin.

Quantity Options Unit temperature -T, -R °C temperature -G files; CSV and VTK output K pressure -P, -R, files, output Pa (300 bar = 300E5) salinity -X, -R, files, output kg NaCl / kg fluid, 0–1 (seawater: 0.032) specific enthalpy -H, -R, files, output J/kg

docs.title: Options of thermo
docs.text:
A value follows its option letter directly or after a space: -P300E5 and -P 300E5 are the same.

Option Meaning -D n required: 0 = single points or a file of points, 1 = profile, 2 = grid, 3 = 3-D grid -V vars required: the varying variables, in order (see the table below) -T, -P, -X, -H fixed values of the variables not in -V (-T and -H exclude each other) -R min/step/max… ranges of the variables in -V, in the same order (-D1 to -D3) -G file file of points (-D0) -O file output file (Output) -F fluid H2O-NaCl (default), H2O or NaCl -B model water model: IAPS84 (default) or IAPWS95 -t n threads; effective only in a library built with -DXTHERMO_OPENMP=ON, otherwise ignored -p show a progress bar (for interactive use on a terminal) -n accepted for compatibility; has no effect -h, -v help, version -D -V Needs 0 PTX or PHX (any order) -T/-H, -P, -X, or a file -G 1 T, P, X or H the two other variables fixed, -R with 3 values, -O 2 PT, PX, TX, PH or HX (either order) the third variable fixed, -R with 6 values 3 PTX or PHX (any order) -R with 9 values; H₂O–NaCl only

Ranges. -Rmin/step/max gives evenly spaced values from min to max, both included: (max − min)/step + 1 points, rounded down, with the spacing adjusted to fit. min must be smaller than max, and the step positive and not larger than max − min. -R1/100/1000 gives 10 values, 111 K apart.

With -F H2O the salinity is 0 and with -F NaCl it is 1, so -X is not needed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Single point from enthalpy:

xThermal thermo -D0 -VPHX -H1500E3 -P316E5 -X0.032

A file of points. Three numbers per line in the order of -V, temperature in kelvin; blank lines are skipped:

points.txt
300E5 573.15 0.1
250E5 673.15 0.032

xThermal thermo -D0 -VPTX -Gpoints.txt -Opoints_result.csv

Profiles at fixed pressure and salinity, in temperature and in enthalpy:

xThermal thermo -D1 -VT -P250E5 -X0.032 -R1/1/1000 -OT_profile.csv
xThermal thermo -D1 -VH -P250E5 -X0.032 -R100E3/10E3/3000E3 -OH_profile.csv

and in pressure and salinity:

xThermal thermo -D1 -VP -T350 -X0.032 -R5E5/5E5/1000E5 -OP_profile.csv
xThermal thermo -D1 -VX -T350 -P250E5 -R0/0.01/1 -OX_profile.csv

Grids: temperature–salinity at 250 bar, and pressure–temperature for seawater:

xThermal thermo -D2 -VTX -R1/5/1000/0/0.01/1 -P250E5 -OTX_250bar.vtk
xThermal thermo -D2 -VPT -R1E5/10E5/1000E5/1/5/800 -X0.032 -OPT_seawater.vtk

A 3-D grid in pressure, temperature and salinity:

xThermal thermo -D3 -VPTX -R100E5/100E5/1000E5/100/50/1000/0/0.05/1 -OPTX.vtk

Pure water with IAPWS-95, and pure NaCl:

xThermal thermo -D0 -VPTX -T380 -P250E5 -FH2O -BIAPWS95
xThermal thermo -D0 -VPTX -T900 -P300E5 -FNaCl

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Mode Output -D0 with -T/-H, -P, -X the property listing on the screen (stdout) -D0 with -G, -D1 a CSV file: -O name, or out_<V>.csv for -G without -O; -D1 requires -O -D2, -D3 a legacy VTK file and a ParaView script (<name>.vtk.py): -O name, or <V>.vtk without -O

CSV files have one row per point. The first columns are T[K], P[Pa], X[kg/kg], then the phase compositions, the phase region (Phase[index], Phase[name]), and the bulk and phase densities, enthalpies, heat capacities, viscosities and saturations. For H₂O–NaCl the saturations Sl[m3/m3], Sv, Sh are volume fractions; for pure water, Sl[kg/kg], Sv are mass fractions. The bulk heat capacity and viscosity of multiphase states follow the definitions on Model and limitations (the viscosity column of a two-phase point holds a placeholder 1).

A CSV name that does not end in .csv gets .csv appended (result.txt gives result.txt.csv). A grid is always written as .vtk: -Ogrid.csv or -Ogrid gives grid.vtk, with a notice.

docs.title: Exit status and errors
docs.text:
Status Meaning 0 success (also -h and -v) 1 the evaluation failed: an input outside the model's range, a state the model cannot evaluate, an unreadable or malformed input file, an unwritable output file 2 the command line cannot be interpreted: an unknown program, option, fluid or water model; a missing or malformed value; a missing required option; an invalid -D, -V or -R; both -T and -H

Errors and warnings go to stderr, results to stdout. A failing point in a file, profile or grid stops the run (status 1, no output file).

xThermal thermo -D0 -VPTX -T1100 -P300E5 -X0.1 || echo "exit status $?"    # above the model's 1000 °C: 1
xThermal thermo -D0 -VPTX -T300 -P300E5 || echo "exit status $?"           # -X missing: 2

The command-line tool checks T, p and X against the model's range before evaluating. Inputs outside the published model domain are rejected there, including pressures below 1 bar, which the library itself would evaluate (see Domain, input checks and errors).

docs.title: Lookup tables
docs.text:
lutgen builds an adaptive lookup table of the properties over a 2-D or 3-D region, lutinfo describes it, lookup evaluates points from it, and lut2vtu converts it for ParaView:

xThermal lutgen -D2 -VXT -R0/0.05/1/100/10/500 -P250E5
xThermal lutinfo lut_constP_XT_6.bin
xThermal lookup lut_constP_XT_6.bin -D0 -VTPX -T300 -P250E5 -X0.1

lutgen writes its files into the current directory, with names from the table type and refinement level (lut_constP_XT_<level>.bin, one file per property, and a .vtu file); it does not use -O. -L sets the minimum refinement level (default 4). Interpolated values from a table are not covered by the verification of the model.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• -t has an effect only in a library built with OpenMP; -n has no effect.
  • The built-in help (-h) still shows some outdated examples and wording; this page is the reference.
  • Error messages for a failed evaluation give the library's explanation but not the input point.

docs.title: Gallery
docs.text:
A few examples of what xThermo computes for hydrothermal fluids. Every figure is made by the Python script shown below it, with the published version of the library; the scripts run in the documentation's test suite. They use the phase-region colours of xthermo.plot_slice and a few shared style settings from docs/gallery/_style.py.

All results come from the H₂O–NaCl model of Driesner & Heinrich (2007) and Driesner (2007) with the IAPS-84 water backend. Where a figure touches a region in which the model's formulation is uncertain, the text says so; the Model and limitations page has the details.

More figures: the homepage (the phase diagram at 250 bar and seawater heated at 250 bar), and the phase diagrams and property maps of the Python guide.

docs.title: How the phase diagram changes with depth
docs.text:
The same temperature–salinity section at four pressures, roughly the pressures at the base of 1, 2.5, 4 and 10 km of seawater. At 100 bar a liquid of seawater salinity (dashed) starts to separate into vapour and brine at 312 °C. Between 341 and 771 °C it is vapour + halite: the brine has dried out and salt precipitates. With rising pressure the two-phase fields move to higher temperatures (separation of seawater at 388 °C at 250 bar, 447 °C at 400 bar and 688 °C at 1000 bar). The three-phase assemblage vapour + liquid + halite exists only up to 390 bar, so at 400 and 1000 bar halite and vapour no longer coexist. The halite liquidus on the salt-rich side (blue) barely moves. The regions are drawn from the library's section geometry, which has a few known inaccuracies (details); none of them affects temperature–salinity sections.

Python code 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

import _style as st                              # fonts and colours of the documentation figures (docs/gallery)

st.apply()
sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
pressures = [100e5, 250e5, 400e5, 1000e5]        # Pa

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13, 4.4), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
handles = {}
for ax, p in zip(axes, pressures):
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    h = xthermo.plot_slice(ax, sw.Slice_constP(p), x="X", y="T", points=False)
    handles.update(h)
    ax.set_xlim(1e-3, 100)                       # wt% NaCl
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1000)                         # °C
    ax.set_title(f"{p / 1e5:.0f} bar", loc="center")
    ax.axvline(3.2, color=st.CORAL, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (5, 3)))   # seawater
    if ax is not axes[0]:
        ax.set_ylabel("")
# one legend entry for the three-phase assemblage (its temperature differs between the panels)
vlh = [k for k in handles if k.startswith("V+L+H")]
handles = {k: v for k, v in handles.items() if k not in vlh} | {"V+L+H (a line in T–X)": handles[vlh[0]]}
fig.legend(handles.values(), handles.keys(), loc="outside lower center", ncol=7, fontsize="small")
fig.suptitle("The H₂O–NaCl phase diagram at four pressures (dashed: seawater, 3.2 wt% NaCl)", x=0.01, ha="left",
             color=st.NAVY, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()

docs.title: Rising seawater: boiling or condensation
docs.text:
Seawater heated at depth rises towards the seafloor and its pressure drops. This example follows three parcels that start at 500 bar and 380, 420 or 450 °C, keeping their specific enthalpy constant as the pressure falls: an idealised, adiabatic ascent with no heat exchanged with the surrounding rock and no change in kinetic or potential energy. Each path is computed with xthermo.hpx at the enthalpy of its starting state.

The two cooler fluids are liquid-like. They reach the two-phase field at 191 and 260 bar (dots) and boil: the vapour fraction grows from zero as the pressure falls, and the fluid cools along the boiling curve. The hottest fluid starts vapour-like (480 kg/m³), close to the critical curve of seawater-like compositions. It enters the two-phase field at 331 bar on the vapour side, so it does not boil: a small amount of brine condenses from it, and the vapour fraction starts near 100 %. At 50 bar all three are vapour + brine at about 266 °C. The library labels all three starting states "Liquid"; above the critical curve this label does not distinguish liquid-like from vapour-like fluids.

The small kinks where the paths cross 374 °C are where the model's vapour–liquid correlations change form at the critical temperature of water. Real upflow exchanges heat with the rock and mixes with other fluids, so these paths show the thermodynamics of decompression, not a model of a vent.

Python code 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

import _style as st                              # fonts and colours of the documentation figures (docs/gallery)

st.apply()
sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
X = 0.032                                        # seawater salinity, kg/kg
p = np.geomspace(500e5, 50e5, 300)               # decompression from 500 to 50 bar, Pa

# where seawater is a single phase or vapour + liquid, in temperature and pressure
T_grid = np.linspace(200, 500, 301) + 273.15
P_grid = np.geomspace(40e5, 550e5, 300)
grid = xthermo.tpx(sw, T_grid[None, :], P_grid[:, None], X, errors="nan")

fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.6), layout="constrained")
ax.set_yscale("log")

docs.title: Coexisting brine and vapour
docs.text:
Inside the vapour + liquid field a fluid splits into a dense, salty brine and a light, nearly salt-free vapour. The figure shows both phases along four isobars. The compositions are the library's V+L compositions (XL_VL, XV_VL), and the densities come from xthermo.tpx at a bulk salinity between the two, which lies inside the two-phase field.

At each pressure the two branches meet at the critical curve, where brine and vapour become identical. Away from it the density contrast, the driving force for the gravitational separation of the two phases, reaches 1000 kg/m³ and more, and the vapour carries orders of magnitude less salt than the brine. At 250 bar the two-phase field is interrupted between 449 and 716 °C, where vapour and halite coexist instead (see the first figure). Higher pressure brings the phases closer: the critical curve moves to higher temperature and the vapour holds more salt.

The figure stops at 800 °C. Above the melting point of NaCl (800.7 °C) the published equation for the vapour composition is incomplete, and xThermo's vapour salinities differ from those of the model author's program by up to about 24 % at 1000 °C (details). Brine densities above 600 °C below 390 bar use the model's high-temperature density extrapolation (extrapolated regions).

Python code 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

import _style as st                              # fonts and colours of the documentation figures (docs/gallery)

st.apply()
sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
T = np.linspace(380, 800, 421) + 273.15          # K; up to 800 °C (see the text)
colours = {250e5: st.CORAL, 400e5: st.TEAL, 600e5: "#1f6f9a", 1000e5: st.NAVY}

fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.6), layout="constrained")
for p, colour in colours.items():
    # compositions of the coexisting liquid and vapour; a bulk salinity between them lies in the two-phase field
    x_l = np.array(sw.XL_VL(T, np.full_like(T, p)))
    x_v = np.array(sw.XV_VL(T, np.full_like(T, p)))
    s = xthermo.tpx(sw, T, p, 0.5 * (x_l + x_v), errors="nan", absent="nan")
    two_phase = s.ok & s.has("liquid") & s.has("vapour") & ~s.has("halite")
    rho_l = np.where(two_phase, s.Rho_l, np.nan)
    rho_v = np.where(two_phase, s.Rho_v, np.nan)
    label = f"{p / 1e5:.0f} bar"
    ax.plot(T - 273.15, rho_l, color=colour, lw=2, label=label)
    ax.plot(T - 273.15, rho_v, color=colour, lw=2, ls="--")
    bx.semilogy(T - 273.15, np.where(two_phase, 100 * s.X_l, np.nan), color=colour, lw=2, label=label)
    bx.semilogy(T - 273.15, np.where(two_phase, 100 * s.X_v, np.nan), color=colour, lw=2, ls="--")

ax.set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
ax.set_ylabel("density (kg/m³)")
ax.set_title("Density: brine (solid) and vapour (dashed)")
ax.legend(fontsize="small")
bx.set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
bx.set_ylabel("salinity (wt% NaCl)")
bx.set_title("Salinity: brine (solid) and vapour (dashed)")
bx.legend(fontsize="small", loc="lower right")
fig.suptitle("Coexisting brine and vapour in the vapour + liquid field of H₂O–NaCl", x=0.01, ha="left",
             color=st.NAVY, fontweight="bold")
plt.show()

docs.title: Water near its critical point
docs.text:
Above its critical pressure (220.6 bar) water passes continuously from a dense, liquid-like state to a light, vapour-like one, without boiling. Where this change is fastest, the heat capacity has a sharp maximum: water then absorbs a lot of heat for a small temperature change. The maximum is highest and narrowest just above the critical pressure (230 bar) and broadens and shifts to higher temperatures with pressure. This matters for heat transport in hydrothermal systems at supercritical conditions.

The two water formulations available in xThermo (solid: IAPS-84, the basis of the H₂O–NaCl model; dotted: IAPWS-95) agree closely except near the maximum at 230 bar, where the peak heights differ by about 10 %. Close to the critical point both are less certain, and the published validity of IAPS-84 excludes a small region around it (details). The peak heights shown also depend on the 0.1 K temperature spacing.

Python code 
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2O

import _style as st                              # fonts and colours of the documentation figures (docs/gallery)

st.apply()
models = {"IAPS-84": H2O.cIAPS84(), "IAPWS-95": H2O.cIAPWS95()}
T = np.linspace(330, 480, 1501) + 273.15         # K, steps of 0.1 K
colours = {230e5: st.CORAL, 250e5: st.TEAL, 300e5: "#1f6f9a", 400e5: st.NAVY}

fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.4), layout="constrained")
for p, colour in colours.items():
    for (name, water), ls in zip(models.items(), ["-", ":"]):
        s = xthermo.tpx(water, T, p, errors="nan")
        label = f"{p / 1e5:.0f} bar" if name == "IAPS-84" else None
        ax.semilogy(T - 273.15, s.Cp / 1e3, color=colour, ls=ls, lw=1.8, label=label)
        bx.plot(T - 273.15, s.Rho, color=colour, ls=ls, lw=1.8, label=label)
ax.set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
ax.set_ylabel("isobaric heat capacity (kJ/(kg K))")
ax.set_title("Heat capacity above the critical pressure")
ax.legend(title="solid: IAPS-84, dotted: IAPWS-95", fontsize="small", title_fontsize="small")
bx.set_xlabel("Temperature (°C)")
bx.set_ylabel("density (kg/m³)")
bx.set_title("Density")
fig.suptitle("Pure water near its critical point (374 °C, 220.6 bar)", x=0.01, ha="left", color=st.NAVY,
             fontweight="bold")
plt.show()

docs.title: The phase diagram in three dimensions
docs.text:
The sections above are slices through one three-dimensional structure in temperature, pressure and salinity. The vapour + liquid region is a dome bounded by its liquid limb (dark grey) and its vapour limb (light grey), which meet along the critical curve (red) on its crest. Below it lies the three-phase surface vapour + liquid + halite, which at each temperature has a single pressure and spans the salinities from the vapour to halite (blue and orange parts). Beneath that, vapour coexists with halite (purple: the vapour side). On the salt-rich side, the halite liquidus (green) separates liquid from liquid + halite.

The salinity axis is linear, so the vapour compositions, often below 0.01 wt% NaCl, lie close to the zero-salinity plane; the sections above show them on a logarithmic axis.

Python code 
import warnings
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
from matplotlib.colors import to_hex
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=RuntimeWarning)
sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")

# ── VLH surface (V→L side and L→H side) ──────────────────────────────────
nT = 80
nT_high = nT // 3
T_high  = H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH + (sw.Tmax_VLH() - H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH) * 0.95
T_vlh   = np.append(np.linspace(H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH, T_high, nT - nT_high),
                    np.linspace(T_high, sw.Tmax_VLH(), nT_high))
P_vlh   = np.array(sw.P_VLH(T_vlh))
Xl_vlh, Xv_vlh = np.array(sw.X_VLH(T_vlh, P_vlh))

n_log, n_lin = 20, 40
nX = n_log + n_lin
TT_vlh = np.tile(T_vlh, (nX, 1))
PP_vlh = np.tile(P_vlh, (nX, 1))
XX_V2L = np.zeros_like(TT_vlh)
XX_L2H = np.zeros_like(TT_vlh)
for j in range(len(T_vlh)):
    XX_V2L[:, j] = np.append(
        10 ** np.linspace(np.log10(max(Xv_vlh[j], 1e-10)), np.log10(0.01), n_log),
        np.linspace(0.01, Xl_vlh[j], n_lin))
    XX_L2H[:, j] = np.linspace(Xl_vlh[j], 1.0, nX)

# ── VH surface ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
nP = 60
T_vh = np.linspace(H2ONaCl.T_MIN_VLH, sw.Tmax_VLH(), nT)
P_vlh2 = np.array(sw.P_VLH(T_vh))
TT_vh = np.tile(T_vh, (nP, 1))
PP_vh = np.zeros_like(TT_vh)
np_low = nP // 3
for i in range(len(T_vh)):
    p_low = sw.pmin() + (P_vlh2[i] - sw.pmin()) * 0.1
    PP_vh[:, i] = np.append(np.linspace(sw.pmin(), p_low, np_low),
                            np.linspace(p_low, P_vlh2[i], nP - np_low))
XX_VH = np.array(sw.X_VH(TT_vh.ravel(), PP_vh.ravel())).reshape(TT_vh.shape)

# ── Halite liquidus ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
TT_lh = np.tile(T_vh, (nP, 1))
PP_lh = np.zeros_like(TT_lh)
for i in range(len(T_vh)):
    PP_lh[:, i] = np.linspace(P_vlh2[i], 2500e5, nP)
XL_LH = np.array(sw.X_HaliteLiquidus(TT_lh.ravel(), PP_lh.ravel())).reshape(TT_lh.shape)

# ── VL surfaces ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
pb_l = sw.PhaseBoundary_VL_DeformLinear(H2ONaCl.Liquid)
pb_v = sw.PhaseBoundary_VL_DeformLinear(H2ONaCl.Vapor)

# ── Critical curve ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
T_crit = np.linspace(sw.get_pWater().T_critical(), sw.Tmax(), 80)
p_crit, X_crit = np.array(sw.P_X_Critical(T_crit))

# ── Plot ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(12, 9))
ax  = fig.add_subplot(111, projection='3d', facecolor='None')
legend = []   # 3-D surfaces give no usable legend handles: one coloured swatch per surface

def surf(TT, PP, XX, color, label):
    ax.plot_surface(XX * 100, TT - 273.15, PP / 1e5,
                    color=color, alpha=0.45, linewidth=0)
    ax.plot_wireframe(XX * 100, TT - 273.15, PP / 1e5,
                      color=color, lw=0.4)
    legend.append(Patch(fc=color, ec=color, alpha=0.6, label=label))

surf(TT_vlh, PP_vlh, XX_V2L,  'steelblue', 'VLH (V side)')
surf(TT_vlh, PP_vlh, XX_L2H,  'orange',    'VLH (L+H side)')
surf(TT_vh,  PP_vh,  XX_VH,   'purple',    'VH surface')
surf(TT_lh,  PP_lh,  XL_LH,   'limegreen', 'Halite liquidus')

for pb, color, label in [(pb_l, 'black', 'VL liquid'), (pb_v, 'gray', 'VL vapor')]:
    T2 = np.array(pb.T); P2 = np.array(pb.p); X2 = np.array(pb.X)
    ax.plot_surface(X2 * 100, T2 - 273.15, P2 / 1e5, color=color, alpha=0.3, linewidth=0)
    ax.plot_wireframe(X2 * 100, T2 - 273.15, P2 / 1e5, color=color, lw=0.4)
    legend.append(Patch(fc=color, ec=color, alpha=0.4, label=label))

ax.plot(X_crit * 100, T_crit - 273.15, p_crit / 1e5, color='red', lw=2)
legend.append(Line2D([], [], color='red', lw=2, label='Critical curve'))
ax.plot(Xv_vlh * 100, T_vlh - 273.15, P_vlh / 1e5, color='red',   lw=1)
ax.plot(Xl_vlh * 100, T_vlh - 273.15, P_vlh / 1e5, color='green', lw=1)

ax.set_xlabel('Salinity (wt% NaCl)', fontsize=10, labelpad=8)
ax.set_ylabel('Temperature (°C)',    fontsize=10, labelpad=8)
ax.set_zlabel('Pressure (bar)',      fontsize=10, labelpad=8)
ax.set_xlim(0, 100); ax.set_ylim(0, 1000); ax.set_zlim(0, 2500)
ax.view_init(elev=25, azim=-145)
ax.set_title(r'H$_2$O–NaCl phase boundaries in T–p–X space', fontsize=13, pad=12)
ax.legend(handles=legend, loc='upper left', fontsize=9)
ax.set_box_aspect(None, zoom=0.88)   # leaves room for the axis labels
plt.show()

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: xThermo is a C++ library with a Python interface. Python users build and install the package xthermo with pip; C++ users build and install the library with CMake. Both compile the library from source, which takes a few minutes.

docs.title: From source (current)
docs.text:
You need Python ≥ 3.10, a C/C++ compiler (gcc ≥ 11 or Apple clang) and make. pip takes CMake and SWIG from PyPI if they are not installed, and builds GSL from the official, checksum-verified release.

git clone https://github.com/lruepke/xThermo.git
cd xThermo
pip install .                 # or: pip install ".[plotting]" to add matplotlib

Use any environment you like (venv, conda, …). NumPy is installed as a dependency; Matplotlib is only needed for the plotting helpers.

Check the installation:

import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, 573.15, 300e5, 0.1)      # T [K], p [Pa], X [kg/kg]
print(xthermo.__version__, s.phase_name, s.Rho)

The former package name still works: from xThermal import H2ONaCl gives the same modules.

pip install xthermo

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
Dependency Required Notes C++ compiler (gcc ≥ 11 or Apple clang) yes the code is compiled as C++11 CMake ≥ 3.18 yes GSL 2.x yes from the system, or built from source by CMake (see below) SWIG ≥ 4 and Python ≥ 3.10 with headers for the Python modules skip with -DXTHERMO_PYTHON=OFF PROST 4.1 bundled the IAPS-84 water backend; compiled automatically

GSL from your package manager:

brew install gsl              # macOS
sudo apt install libgsl-dev   # Debian/Ubuntu
conda install -c conda-forge gsl

For a GSL in a non-standard location add -DGSL_ROOT_DIR=<prefix>. Without a system GSL, add -DXTHERMO_BUNDLED_GSL=ON: CMake then downloads the official GSL 2.8 release from ftp.gnu.org, checks its SHA-256 checksum and builds it. For offline builds, point -DXTHERMO_GSL_ARCHIVE=<path to gsl-2.8.tar.gz> to a local copy of the same archive.

docs.title: Build and install
docs.text:
From the repository root:

cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=install
cmake --build build -j
cmake --install build

The build type is Release unless -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE is given. Options:

Option Default Description XTHERMO_PYTHON ON Build the Python modules (SWIG) XTHERMO_BUNDLED_GSL OFF Build the pinned GSL release from source instead of using the system GSL XTHERMO_OPENMP OFF Use OpenMP for batch and lookup-table evaluation BUILD_SHARED_LIBS OFF Build the C++ library as a shared library XTHERMO_BUILD_TESTS OFF Build the developer test programs (ctest)

cmake --install creates:

install/
├── bin/xThermal                 # command-line tool
├── include/xThermo/             # C++ headers
├── lib/libxThermal.a            # C++ library
├── lib/cmake/xThermo/           # CMake package: find_package(xThermo)

docs.title: Model, verification and limitations
docs.text: xThermo computes the properties of H₂O–NaCl fluids with the correlations of Driesner & Heinrich (2007) and Driesner (2007), combined with an equation of state for pure water. This page explains the model, what has been verified and what that verification means, where xThermo deliberately differs from other implementations, how the properties of multiphase states are defined, and which limitations are known.

docs.title: In brief
docs.text:
• The model is a set of empirical correlations fitted to experimental data from 0 to 1000 °C, 1 to 5000 bar and 0 to 1 mole fraction NaCl. Densities and enthalpies of brines are obtained from those of pure water at a scaled temperature. The correlations were fitted with the IAPS-84 equation of state for water, xThermo's reference backend.
  • Verification shows that xThermo reproduces the model author's published tables and equations, apart from documented differences. It does not show that the model is accurate: that rests on the authors' comparison with experiments.
  • Three deliberate differences from the author's own program concern hot, saline liquids at low pressure (enthalpy, up to about 3 %), vapour compositions above 800.7 °C (up to about 24 %) and the heat capacity of saline phases (by a factor 1/(1 + x)). xThermo follows the published equations and keeps heat capacity consistent with enthalpy.
  • Bulk properties of multiphase states are defined below. The bulk heat capacity contains no latent heat, and the bulk viscosity is not defined; use the phase properties.
  • Known limitations include extrapolated regions, a few confirmed numerical defects with small or local effects, and open questions near the melting point of pure NaCl.

docs.title: Phase relations
docs.text: Driesner & Heinrich (2007) give correlations in temperature, pressure and NaCl mole fraction for every phase boundary of the system: the melting, sublimation and boiling curves of NaCl, the critical curve, the halite liquidus, the three-phase surface vapour + liquid + halite (V+L+H), the compositions of halite-saturated vapour, and the liquid and vapour compositions of the vapour + liquid (V+L) region. Together they define which phases are present at a given temperature, pressure and bulk composition. The Gallery shows the resulting phase diagram at four pressures and in three dimensions.

docs.title: Volumetric and thermal properties
docs.text: Driesner (2007) gives the molar volume, specific enthalpy and isobaric heat capacity of the liquid and vapour phases with a scaled temperature (corresponding-temperature) method. A brine at temperature T, pressure p and composition x is given the molar volume of pure water at the same pressure and a scaled temperature T*_V(T, p, x). In the same way its specific enthalpy is that of pure water at a second scaled temperature T*_h, and the heat capacity is the temperature derivative of that enthalpy. Pure-water properties come from the water equation of state. Where the scaled temperature falls outside the range in which water properties can be used, the volume correlation is extrapolated: at low pressure near boiling, and above about 600 °C below 390 bar. Halite has its own correlations for density and enthalpy.

docs.title: Viscosity
docs.text: The viscosity of brines follows Klyukin et al. (2017), which also evaluates the viscosity of water at a transformed temperature. Water viscosity comes from the IAPWS 2008 formulation with the IAPWS-95 backend and from the NBS/NRC Steam Tables correlation (as implemented in PROST) with the IAPS-84 backend.

docs.title: Water backends
docs.text:
Backend Formulation Range of the pure-water class "IAPS84" (default of the command-line tool) IAPS-84 (Haar, Gallagher & Kell 1984; Kestin & Sengers 1986), computed with PROST 4.1 260–2500 K, up to 30 000 bar "IAPWS95" IAPWS-95 (Wagner & Pruß 2002) 273.165–2273.15 K, up to 5000 bar
  • The Driesner correlations were fitted with IAPS-84. "IAPS84" is therefore the reference backend; results with "IAPWS95" are a variant of the model, not a separate validation of it.
  • Most phase-boundary correlations do not depend on the backend, for example the V+L+H pressure, and the critical curve above 500 °C.
  • Below 500 °C the critical curve uses the critical point of the selected water backend. With "IAPWS95" the critical pressure is up to about 0.07 % higher, and the curve has a step of about 0.03 % at 500 °C.
  • V+L vapour compositions differ between the backends by about 1 % between 300 and 450 °C, and by more at lower temperatures and close to the boiling pressure of water, where the vapour salinity tends to zero.
  • Densities, enthalpies and heat capacities of brines differ slightly, because they are evaluated through the water equation of state.
  • Any other backend name raises NotImplementedError.

docs.title: Model domain
docs.text: The correlations are published for 0–1000 °C, 1–5000 bar and X_NaCl = 0–1. The H₂O–NaCl class reports this domain as Tmin() = 273.16 K, Tmax() = 1273.15 K, pmin() = 1e5 Pa and pmax() = 5e8 Pa. Which inputs outside it are rejected is listed under Domain, input checks and errors.

docs.title: What was compared
docs.text:
• The author's published tables. The electronic supplements of both papers tabulate phase boundaries, coexisting compositions, densities and enthalpies. xThermo with IAPS-84 was compared with all ten tables: 29 680 values in 24 comparisons, one per tabulated quantity. 13 of the 24 agree to the printed precision. In the other 11, the differences at individual states are each traced to a cause: the deliberate differences described below, the other GEOMAR modifications, the defects at the saturation pressure of pure water, or table entries that are inconsistent with the published equations themselves (for example four liquid enthalpies that are exactly one tenth of the equation's value). Eight marginal rows, within 1.1 times the tolerance, remain without a diagnosed cause.
  • The published equations, evaluated independently. Wherever the papers give a single explicit formula, evaluating it directly with IAPS-84 reproduces the tables to their printed seven digits. This shows that the tables are a sound reference there.
  • The author's program SoWat 0.2 (2009), at selected states.
  • The water equations of state. IAPWS-95 reproduces the verification tables of the IAPWS release, the tables of Wagner & Pruß (2002) and an independent implementation, for density, enthalpy and density derivatives to round-off; its viscosity reproduces the check values of the IAPWS 2008 viscosity release. For IAPS-84, the publication (Kestin & Sengers 1986) tabulates check values only for pressure, isochoric heat capacity and the Helmholtz function: pressure and heat capacity are reproduced to the printed digits, the Helmholtz function up to the reference-state adjustment that the release allows.
  • Internal consistency. Heat capacities equal the temperature derivative of the enthalpy (to 1e-5), density derivatives are consistent with the density, and enthalpy-based input (H–p–X) returns the temperature of the corresponding T–p–X state. Exceptions are listed under Known limitations.

The comparisons run as automated tests in the development repository; they are not part of the public source snapshot.

docs.title: What the agreement means
docs.text: Agreement with the published tables shows that xThermo implements the author's formulation as published. It is not an estimate of experimental accuracy. The accuracy of the model against experimental data is the one reported by its authors, for example an uncertainty of 0.1–0.2 % in density at low temperature and pressure, and an overestimate of the heat capacity by up to 10 % at high temperature and salinity (Driesner 2007). Disagreement with an individual table entry does not by itself prove an error in xThermo, because a few entries are inconsistent with the published equations.

docs.title: What has not been verified
docs.text:
• the viscosity of brines (Klyukin et al. 2017) and the IAPS-84 water viscosity;
  • the properties of halite and of liquid NaCl;
  • density derivatives and heat capacities against experimental data;
  • the phase region away from the tabulated states (the tables lie almost entirely on phase boundaries);
  • IAPS-84 beyond its published check values;
  • results with the IAPWS-95 backend against the author's tables, which were computed with IAPS-84.

docs.title: Differences from the published formulation
docs.text: Other implementations of the same model include the author's SoWat program, his tabulated supplementary data, ProBrine and earlier GEOMAR MATLAB code. Three differences between them and xThermo are known and were decided after a scientific assessment. Questions about the author's undocumented treatments remain open; the decisions can be revisited if he clarifies them.

docs.title: Heat capacity
docs.text:
• xThermo: c_P = (∂h/∂T)_{p,x}, the published Eq. 27 of Driesner (2007). It is consistent with the enthalpy.
  • SoWat 0.2 and ProBrine multiply Eq. 27 by 1/(1 + x), where x is the NaCl mole fraction of the phase, and leave the enthalpy unchanged. SoWat describes the factor as missed in the original publication; no derivation of it has been published.
  • Applied to c_P alone, the factor makes c_P inconsistent with the enthalpy. It is not a change of units or composition basis, and the authors' own comparison with experimental data does not indicate a need for a correction of this form. It has not been tested against experimental data here.
  • Consequence: SoWat and ProBrine heat capacities of saline phases are lower by the factor 1/(1 + x): about 1 % for seawater, 9 % at 26 wt% NaCl, 23 % at 58 wt% and up to 50 % for nearly pure NaCl liquid.

docs.title: Liquid enthalpy of hot brines at low pressure
docs.text:
• This applies to the liquid at T ≥ 600 °C and p ≤ 390.147 bar. There, the published enthalpy correlation can map the brine onto a water state in the vapour field, where it is not usable.
  • xThermo uses a smooth extrapolation constructed at GEOMAR. It has the same form as the published density extrapolation for this region, is continuous at 390.147 bar, and its heat capacity is consistent with it. Elsewhere it reproduces the published equation.
  • It differs from the author's tabulated values by up to about 3 % (median 0.8 %), which corresponds to −19 to +28 K in the temperature of a given enthalpy. The author's treatment in this region is not described in the paper, and none of the forms tested reproduces it.
  • This is a difference between two implementations that both extrapolate beyond the fitted data. The physical accuracy of either in this region has not been established.

docs.title: Vapour composition above the melting point of NaCl
docs.text:
• Above the triple point of NaCl (800.7 °C), the published vapour-composition equation (Driesner & Heinrich 2007, Eq. 15) contains a term that is not defined.
  • xThermo sets it to 1. This is consistent with the published condition that the boiling curve of NaCl bounds the V+L field from below.
  • The author's program uses an undocumented, temperature-dependent value instead. Against it, xThermo's vapour NaCl content is about 1.3 % lower at 810 °C, 6–13 % lower at 850–900 °C and up to about 24 % lower at 1000 °C (12 % at 1000 bar). The absolute amounts are small: below 300 bar the vapour carries 0.01–0.2 wt% NaCl.
  • Below 800.7 °C, xThermo reproduces the author's tabulated compositions.
  • Available experimental data do not decide between the two treatments.

docs.title: Other modifications
docs.text:
These were introduced in the GEOMAR implementations from which xThermo was ported, or in the port itself. The sizes are differences from the published equations or the author's tables at the tested states.

Modification Effect The low-temperature correction term D(T) of the density mapping (Driesner 2007, Eq. 13) is left out, because it can push the scaled temperature below the freezing point of water brine density lower by up to 0.18 % at 10–50 °C and 500–2000 bar near halite saturation; ≤ 0.01 % above about 50 °C Molar mass of water 18.015268 g/mol instead of the paper's 18.015 g/mol ≤ 1.5e-5 in density and in conversions between mass and mole fraction Low-pressure density extrapolation (Eq. 17) in a different working form; the printed equation is ambiguous brine density 0.16–0.46 % off at 1–15 bar near boiling, up to 3 % below 1 bar High-temperature, low-pressure density extrapolation (Eq. 18) with the region clarified by the author in 2018; working form not reproduced exactly ≤ 0.06 % for hot, salt-rich liquids Liquid branch of the V+L surface above 800.7 °C anchored at zero pressure instead of on the NaCl boiling curve ≤ 1e-5 in liquid composition The 900 °C upper bound of PROST's water viscosity is not applied above 900 °C the IAPS-84 viscosity is an extrapolation; it differs from the IAPWS 2008 formulation by −0.4 to +6.1 % at 900–1100 °C

docs.title: Multiphase properties
docs.text:
Each phase has its own (intrinsic) properties: Rho_l, H_l, Cp_l, Mu_l, X_l for the liquid, _v for the vapour and _h for halite. They are computed from the published correlations at the phase's own composition. The bulk fields describe the mixture:

Field Single phase Two or three phases S_l, S_v, S_h 1 for the present phase volume fractions of the phases (H₂O–NaCl). The pure-water classes in xthermo.H2O report the vapour mass fraction instead. Rho phase density Σ S_i ρ_i H phase enthalpy mass-weighted: Σ S_i ρ_i h_i / ρ Cp (∂h/∂T)_{p,x} of the phase frozen heat capacity: Σ S_i ρ_i c_P,i / ρ, at fixed phase amounts and compositions; 0 in V+L+H IsothermalCompressibility of the phase equilibrium compressibility in V+L, V+H and L+H: from the bulk density at fixed T and bulk composition, with the phases re-equilibrating; 0 in V+L+H IsobaricExpansivity, dRhodT, dRhodP of the phase not computed (0); use the phase fields *_l, *_v Mu phase viscosity not defined: a placeholder value of 1 in V+L, V+H and L+H. Two enthalpy-based paths set S_l μ_l + S_v μ_v instead: V+L+H, and V+L of pure water. Use Mu_l and Mu_v.

Frozen and equilibrium heat capacity. In a multiphase state the enthalpy of the mixture also changes because mass moves between phases of different enthalpy (latent heat) and because the coexisting compositions change with temperature. The equilibrium heat capacity (∂H/∂T)_{p,X} contains these terms; the bulk Cp does not. Near phase boundaries the difference is large. In V+L at 400 °C, 250 bar and 10 wt% NaCl, Cp is 9.2 kJ/(kg K), whereas the temperature derivative of the bulk enthalpy is 31 kJ/(kg K):

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")
dT = 0.01                                            # K
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, 673.15 + np.array([-dT, 0.0, dT]), 250e5, 0.10)
print(s.phase_name[1])                               # V+L
print(s.Cp[1] / 1e3)                                 # frozen: 9.2 kJ/(kg K)
print((s.H[2] - s.H[0]) / (2 * dT) / 1e3)            # equilibrium (dH/dT): 31 kJ/(kg K)

How bulk heat capacity and bulk viscosity of multiphase states should be defined is an open question; the effective properties of a multiphase flow (viscosity, relative permeability, storage terms) belong to the flow model. The fields above may change when it is decided.

Saturation and phase-amount conventions. The H₂O–NaCl saturations are volume fractions. The pure-water classes report the vapour mass fraction (quality) in S_v; convert with w_v = S_v ρ_v / ρ when you combine the two. The pure-water classes leave the bulk two-phase Cp at 0.

Absent phases. Fields of a phase that is not present keep 0 in the C++ structure and the classic interface; xthermo.tpx and xthermo.hpx can return NaN for them instead (absent="nan"; see Evaluating states).

docs.title: Domain, input checks and errors
docs.text:
Only part of the model domain is enforced at run time:

Input Behaviour T above 1273.15 K, or H above the enthalpy at 1273.15 K (H₂O–NaCl) OutOfRangeError non-finite T, p, H or X; p ≤ 0; X < 0 InvalidInputError p < 1 bar not checked: values are extrapolations of the correlations p > 5000 bar "IAPS84": not checked, values are returned; "IAPWS95": OutOfRangeError from the water backend X > 1 not checked: values are returned (X = 1.2 gives an "L+H" state), but they have no physical meaning

Results outside the published domain have not been validated. Check your inputs before calling the library.

When an evaluation fails, the library raises a typed error rather than returning a previous or partial state. In C++ the errors derive from xThermal::xThermalBaseError. In Python they are subclasses of xthermo.EvaluationError: InvalidInputError (bad input), OutOfRangeError (outside the range the model or backend can evaluate), NotConvergedError (a numerical solution failed) and NotAvailableError (not provided for this model or state). The C++ functions tryUpdateState_TPX and tryUpdateState_HPX return an EvaluationStatus instead of throwing.

Array evaluation. xthermo.tpx and xthermo.hpx raise the first error by default (errors="raise"). With errors="nan" they evaluate every point, set the failed points to NaN and report each point's outcome in a Status array, so that valid points are kept. See Errors and status.

Individual properties. A property that cannot be evaluated at an otherwise valid state is NaN, while the other properties remain valid: for example the IAPS-84 water viscosity outside its validity range (above 5000 bar, above 3500 bar at temperatures over 150 °C, and above 3000 bar over 600 °C), and brine viscosities that depend on it.

Phase-boundary functions. Some helpers do not raise outside their own temperature range; they print a warning and return 0 (for example X_Critical for temperatures outside the critical curve).

docs.title: Limitations of the published correlations
docs.text:
• Extrapolated regions. Densities of brines below about 15 bar near boiling, and densities and liquid enthalpies above about 600 °C below 390 bar, come from extrapolations (see above). Pressures below 1 bar are outside the model.
  • Negative compressibility of some saline liquids near 1 bar. The published density correlation gives a negative isothermal compressibility for stable, single-phase or halite-saturated liquids at about ≤ 5 bar, 10–100 °C and salinities above about three quarters of halite saturation (for example −3e-5 per bar at 50 °C and 1 bar, near halite saturation). A stable phase requires a positive compressibility, so the correlation is not thermodynamically consistent in this corner. The effect on density is about 2e-5 relative, within the stated uncertainty of the correlation. xThermo keeps the published correlation unchanged; its derivatives are consistent with the density it returns.
  • Near the critical point of water the IAPS-84 formulation is excluded from its published range of validity, and both water formulations are less certain. Dilute brines inherit this through the scaled temperature.
  • Vapour composition above 800.7 °C and the liquid enthalpy of hot brines at low pressure are uncertain, as described above.

docs.title: Confirmed numerical defects
docs.text:
These are known, reproducible and open. Their effects are small or local; workarounds are given where they exist.

  • Section geometry (Slice_constP, Slice_constT, and the plotting functions that use them). Each state is computed correctly by tpx and hpx; only the drawn regions are affected.
    • In isobaric enthalpy–salinity sections below about 221 bar, a thin sliver of the V+L region at salinities below 0.13 wt% NaCl is missing.
    • In isothermal sections, the liquid + halite region continues below the three-phase pressure, where vapour + halite is stable. The plotting functions draw vapour + halite on top, so their figures are correct.
    • Isothermal sections below 374 °C contain a spurious "critical point" at X = 0.
  • Pure water exactly at its saturation pressure (within about one part in a million).
    • With IAPS-84, the phase label and the density can belong to different phases (at 150 °C, a state labelled "Vapor" with the liquid density), and states inside the backend's two-phase tolerance are evaluated 0.1 K away from the requested temperature. Vapour densities step by up to 0.37 % there.
    • With IAPWS-95 the evaluation fails with NotConvergedError.
  • IAPWS-95 brines at low temperature and at 5000 bar. With the IAPWS-95 backend, brines below about 7 °C (10 wt% NaCl) to about 21 °C (50 wt%) cannot be evaluated, because the scaled temperature falls below the range of the water formulation (OutOfRangeError). At exactly 5000 bar, brines of 30 wt% NaCl and more fail below 129 °C (30 wt%) to 238 °C (50 wt% and more) as well, while 4999.99 bar works. IAPS-84 evaluates both.
  • Density derivatives in the low-pressure extrapolation. At 1–5 bar near boiling, ∂ρ/∂p of brines is off by up to −46 % and has the wrong sign at 70 °C and 1 bar; ∂ρ/∂T is within 0.1 %. The density itself is unaffected.
  • Density noise with IAPWS-95 at high temperature and low pressure. In the high-temperature extrapolation, brine densities with IAPWS-95 show small jumps of about 6e-4 relative, and ∂ρ/∂T is rough to about 1e-3. IAPS-84 is not affected.
  • Liquid enthalpy below 1 bar. The extrapolation used when the scaled temperature of the liquid enthalpy falls into the vapour field of water uses a density where an enthalpy is intended. Inside 1–5000 bar it is not reached for liquids that exist; it gives wrong values below 1 bar (up to +250 % at 30–60 °C) and for direct phase-property calls at states where no liquid exists.

docs.title: Under investigation
docs.text:
These are reproducible observations whose cause or correct treatment has not been established. Both concern pure NaCl (X = 1) near its melting point.

  • Enthalpy-based input inside the melting range. For pure NaCl, enthalpies between those of halite and of the liquid at the melting temperature correspond to halite and liquid coexisting. hpx returns such a state as successful, but with a different enthalpy: at 250 bar, an input of 1.031 MJ/kg gives an L+H state at 806.9 °C with H = 0.807 MJ/kg, 22 % lower. Elsewhere, the returned enthalpy equals the input to within 1e-6. Do not rely on hpx for pure NaCl inside its melting range.
  • Enthalpy of liquid NaCl and halite. At the melting point the enthalpy of pure NaCl rises from the halite value to the liquid value, by 0.25 MJ/kg at 1 bar (0.79 to 1.04 MJ/kg). Liquid NaCl is computed with the brine correlations at X = 1, halite with its own correlation; the halite enthalpy's reference value has not been traced to a published source. Whether the two enthalpies share a reference state, and whether the step agrees with the heat of fusion of the published formulation, has not been checked. The properties of pure NaCl have not been independently verified.

docs.title: C++ API overview
docs.text: xThermo is a C++ library; the Python package and the command-line tool are built on the same classes. This guide covers the stable public interface: constructing a model, evaluating states, handling errors, and using the library from several threads. The model itself, its verification and its limitations are described on Model and limitations.

docs.title: Installing the library
docs.text:
Build and install xThermo with CMake (details and options on Installation):

cmake -S . -B build
cmake --build build
cmake --install build --prefix "$HOME/opt/xthermo"

The installation contains the headers in <prefix>/include/xThermo/, the library libxThermal in <prefix>/lib/, the command-line tool xThermal in <prefix>/bin/, and a CMake package in <prefix>/lib/cmake/xThermo/.

docs.title: Using xThermo in a CMake project
docs.text:
find_package(xThermo) provides the target xThermo::xThermal, which carries the include directory and the GSL dependency. A complete project has two files:

CMakeLists.txt
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
project(my_app LANGUAGES CXX)

find_package(xThermo REQUIRED)

add_executable(my_app main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(my_app PRIVATE xThermo::xThermal)
main.cpp
#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    xThermal::H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl brine("IAPS84");                        // H2O-NaCl with the IAPS-84 water model
    xThermal::ThermodynamicProperties s = brine.UpdateState_TPX(300 + 273.15, 300e5, 0.1);   // T [K], p [Pa], X [kg/kg]
    std::cout << brine.phase_name(s.phase) << ", " << s.Rho << " kg/m3\n";                   // Liquid, 849.034 kg/m3
}

Configure with the installation prefix in CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH, then build and run:

cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="$HOME/opt/xthermo"
cmake --build build
./build/my_app

The test suite builds this project against a fresh installation.

Compiling without CMake

The library needs the GSL. With a system GSL (gsl-config in the PATH):

g++ -std=c++11 -I"$HOME/opt/xthermo/include/xThermo" $(gsl-config --cflags) -o my_app main.cpp \
    -L"$HOME/opt/xthermo/lib" -lxThermal $(gsl-config --libs)

If xThermo was built with -DXTHERMO_BUNDLED_GSL=ON, the GSL is installed with it: use -I<prefix>/lib/xThermo/gsl/include and -L<prefix>/lib/xThermo/gsl/lib -lgsl -lgslcblas instead of gsl-config. CMake does this for you.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
Class Model Construction xThermal::H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl H₂O–NaCl (Driesner & Heinrich 2007; Driesner 2007) cH2ONaCl brine("IAPS84") or ("IAPWS95"): the water model used inside xThermal::PROST::cIAPS84 pure water, IAPS-84 cIAPS84 water; xThermal::IAPWS95::cIAPWS95 pure water, IAPWS-95 cIAPWS95 water; xThermal::NaCl::cNaCl pure NaCl cNaCl salt("IAPS84");

Including H2ONaCl.h makes all four available. All derive from xThermal::cxThermal, so a function can take any model as cxThermal&. An unknown water-model name throws NotImplementedError at construction. "IAPS84" is the reference: the H₂O–NaCl correlations were fitted with it (see Water backends).

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
All functions use SI units, with temperature in kelvin:

Quantity Unit temperature T K pressure p Pa salinity X kg NaCl / kg fluid (mass fraction, 0–1) specific enthalpy H J/kg density kg/m³ heat capacity J/(kg K) viscosity Pa s

Tmin(), Tmax(), pmin() and pmax() give the range a model declares: for H₂O–NaCl 273.16–1273.15 K and 1e5–5e8 Pa. Which inputs outside it are rejected is listed under Errors and threads.

docs.title: In this guide
docs.text:
• Evaluating states: T–p–X and H–p–X evaluation, single points and batches, the result fields
  • Errors and threads: exceptions, status codes, thread safety, OpenMP
  • Phase region: the phase of a state without evaluating its properties
  • Phase boundaries: the critical curve, the three-phase surface, coexisting compositions

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
When a state cannot be evaluated, UpdateState_TPX and UpdateState_HPX throw an exception derived from xThermal::xThermalBaseError (itself a std::exception; what() gives the message, code() the error code). The library does not return a previous state, a partial result or default values instead.

Exception Cause EvaluationStatus InputError (a ValueError) non-finite T, H, p or X; p ≤ 0; X < 0 InvalidInput OutOfRangeError outside the range in which the model evaluates, e.g. T above 1273.15 K for H₂O–NaCl OutOfRange SolutionError a numerical solution failed, e.g. IAPWS-95 water exactly at its saturation pressure NotConverged NotImplementedError, NotAvailableError not provided for this model or state, e.g. H–p–X for pure NaCl NotAvailable other xThermalBaseError (e.g. ValueError) any other error reported by the library Failed 
#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl brine("IAPS84");
    ThermodynamicProperties props;
    try {
        brine.UpdateState_TPX(props, 1100 + 273.15, 300e5, 0.1);         // above the model's 1000 °C
    } catch (const OutOfRangeError& e) {
        std::cout << "out of range\n";
    } catch (const xThermalBaseError& e) {                               // any other failure
        std::cout << evaluation_status_name(evaluation_status(e.code())) << ": " << e.what() << "\n";
    }
}

docs.title: Status codes
docs.text:
tryUpdateState_* and the batch functions evaluate_* report the same failures as an EvaluationStatus (Evaluating states). evaluation_status(e.code()) converts an exception's code, and evaluation_status_name(status) gives its name ("OutOfRange" for EvaluationStatus::OutOfRange). In the batch results, status[i] holds the value as an integer:

Value EvaluationStatus Python (xthermo.Status) 0 Ok Ok 1 InvalidInput InvalidInput 2 OutOfRange OutOfRange 3 NotConverged NotConverged 4 NotAvailable NotAvailable 5 Failed Failed

Errors that are not evaluation failures (for example std::bad_alloc) are not converted into a status; they propagate from every function.

docs.title: Input checks
docs.text:
Every evaluation rejects non-finite inputs, p ≤ 0 and X < 0 (InputError), and H₂O–NaCl temperatures above 1273.15 K (OutOfRangeError). Other inputs outside the published model domain (0–1000 °C, 1–5000 bar, X 0–1) are not all rejected: pressures below 1 bar, and X above 1, are evaluated as extrapolations. Check inputs against the domain where it matters; Domain, input checks and errors has the full list.

A single property that cannot be evaluated at an otherwise valid state is NaN, and the other properties remain valid (Result fields).

docs.title: Threads
docs.text:
A model object is not thread-safe. Code that evaluates states concurrently needs one model object per thread. Independent objects share no state and give the same results as a serial evaluation. Construct a new object per thread rather than copying one:

#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>
#include <vector>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    std::vector<double> T = {300 + 273.15, 350 + 273.15, 400 + 273.15, 450 + 273.15};   // K
    std::vector<double> rho(T.size());
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < T.size(); i++)
        threads.emplace_back([i, &T, &rho]() {
            H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl brine("IAPS84");        // one model per thread
            rho[i] = brine.UpdateState_TPX(T[i], 300e5, 0.1).Rho;
        });
    for (auto& t : threads) t.join();
    for (double r : rho) std::cout << r << " kg/m3\n";
}

MPI ranks have their own objects anyway. In OpenMP code of your own, create the model inside the parallel region.

Internal OpenMP (optional). A library built with -DXTHERMO_OPENMP=ON can evaluate the vector functions (evaluate_* and the vector UpdateState_*) in parallel: model.set_num_threads(n) sets the number of threads for that object. It creates one model per thread itself and gives the same results as a serial evaluation. The default is 1 thread, and the build option is off by default. Without it, set_num_threads has no effect and get_num_threads() returns 1. In a program that is already parallel (a simulator with MPI or its own threads), keep the internal threading off.

docs.title: VLH coexistence pressure
docs.text:
P_VLH returns the pressure on the three-phase V+L+H surface for a given temperature.

#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl eos("IAPS84");

    int N = 100;
    double T_min = H2ONaCl::T_MIN_VLH;
    double T_max = H2ONaCl::T_MAX_VLH;
    double dT = (T_max - T_min) / (N - 1);

    std::cout << "T(°C)    P_VLH(bar)\n";
    for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
        double T = T_min + i * dT;   // K
        double P = eos.P_VLH(T);     // Pa
        std::cout << T - 273.15 << "    " << P / 1e5 << "\n";
    }
}

docs.title: Critical curve
docs.text:
#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl eos("IAPS84");

    double T = 500 + 273.15;   // K
    double P_crit, X_crit;
    eos.P_X_Critical(T, P_crit, X_crit);   // P_crit [Pa], X_crit [kg/kg]
    std::cout << P_crit / 1e5 << " bar, " << X_crit << " kg/kg\n";
}

docs.title: VLH liquid and vapour compositions
docs.text:
#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl eos("IAPS84");

    double T = 600 + 273.15;   // K, within [T_MIN_VLH, T_MAX_VLH]
    double P = eos.P_VLH(T);
    double X_L, X_V;
    eos.X_VLH(T, P, X_L, X_V);   // X_L: liquid (halite liquidus), X_V: vapour [kg/kg]
    std::cout << P / 1e5 << " bar: X_L = " << X_L << ", X_V = " << X_V << "\n";
}

docs.title: Phase region
docs.text:
findPhaseRegion_TPX returns the phase region index without computing all thermodynamic properties.

#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl eos("IAPS84");

    double T = 400 + 273.15;   // K
    double p = 200e5;           // Pa  (200 bar)
    double X = 0.032;           // kg/kg  (3.2 wt% NaCl)

    PhaseRegion region = eos.findPhaseRegion_TPX(T, p, X);
    std::string name = eos.phase_name(region);

    std::cout << "Phase region: " << name << " (index " << region << ")\n";
}

docs.title: Phase region names
docs.text:
Names returned by phase_name for H₂O–NaCl states:

Name Enum value Description Liquid SinglePhase_L Single liquid phase. Single-phase "liquid-like" and "vapour-like" fluid above the critical curve are also reported as Liquid. Vapor SinglePhase_V Single vapour phase V+L TwoPhase_VL Vapour–liquid coexistence L+H TwoPhase_LH Liquid–halite coexistence V+H TwoPhase_VH Vapour–halite coexistence V+L+H ThreePhase_VLH Three-phase coexistence (reached through the H–p–X flash)

For pure water, the names of the water backend are used instead, for example Supercritical and Sup.crit. liquid, and V+L(water) in the two-phase region. This applies to the pure-water classes and also to cH2ONaCl at X = 0, which evaluates pure water directly.

docs.title: Phase name from an UpdateState result
docs.text:
#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl eos("IAPS84");
    ThermodynamicProperties props;
    eos.UpdateState_TPX(props, 400 + 273.15, 250e5, 0.1);
    std::cout << eos.phase_name(props.phase) << "\n";   // V+L
}

docs.title: Evaluating states
docs.text:
A state is given by temperature, pressure and bulk salinity (T–p–X), or by specific enthalpy, pressure and salinity (H–p–X). Every model offers the same functions:

Function Input On failure UpdateState_TPX(props, T, p, X), UpdateState_HPX(props, H, p, X) one state; fills props throws (see Errors and threads) UpdateState_TPX(T, p, X), UpdateState_HPX(H, p, X) one state; returns the properties throws tryUpdateState_TPX(props, T, p, X, &message), tryUpdateState_HPX(...) one state returns an EvaluationStatus evaluate_TPX(T, p, X), evaluate_HPX(H, p, X) vectors of points records a status per point UpdateState_TPX(T, p, X), UpdateState_HPX(H, p, X) with vectors vectors of points throws at the first failing point

For pure water and pure NaCl, X is ignored (it may be omitted).

docs.title: One state
docs.text:
#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl brine("IAPS84");

    ThermodynamicProperties props;
    brine.UpdateState_TPX(props, 400 + 273.15, 250e5, 0.032);   // T [K], p [Pa], X [kg/kg]: seawater at 400 °C, 250 bar

    std::cout << brine.phase_name(props.phase) << "\n"          // V+L
              << "bulk density " << props.Rho << " kg/m3\n"     // 194.068
              << "liquid: " << props.Rho_l << " kg/m3, X_l = " << props.X_l << "\n"
              << "vapour: " << props.Rho_v << " kg/m3, X_v = " << props.X_v << "\n"
              << "vapour volume fraction " << props.S_v << "\n";

    // the same state from its enthalpy: T is a result
    ThermodynamicProperties same = brine.UpdateState_HPX(props.H, 250e5, 0.032);
    std::cout << "T = " << same.T - 273.15 << " °C\n";          // 400
}

Each call resets the result object, so no value of a previous call survives in props.

docs.title: Without exceptions
docs.text:
tryUpdateState_TPX and tryUpdateState_HPX evaluate the same state but return its outcome instead of throwing. On failure the inputs are kept, every other number is NaN, the phase is Unknown, and the optional message receives the library's explanation:

#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl brine("IAPS84");
    ThermodynamicProperties props;
    std::string message;

    EvaluationStatus status = brine.tryUpdateState_TPX(props, 1100 + 273.15, 300e5, 0.1, &message);
    if (status != EvaluationStatus::Ok)
        std::cout << evaluation_status_name(status) << "\n";   // OutOfRange: above 1000 °C
    std::cout << props.Rho << "\n";                              // nan
}

The statuses are listed under Errors and threads.

docs.title: Many states
docs.text:
evaluate_TPX and evaluate_HPX take vectors of equal length (point i is T[i], p[i], X[i]) and never stop at a failing point. The result holds one vector per field, status[i] (0 = ok) and the messages of the failed points in failed_message, in index order:

#include "H2ONaCl.h"
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

using namespace xThermal;

int main()
{
    H2ONaCl::cH2ONaCl brine("IAPS84");
    std::vector<double> T = {300 + 273.15, 2000, 400 + 273.15};   // K; the second point is above the model's range
    std::vector<double> p = {300e5, 300e5, 250e5};                 // Pa
    std::vector<double> X = {0.1, 0.1, 0.032};                     // kg/kg

    ThermodynamicPropertiesVector r = brine.evaluate_TPX(T, p, X);
    for (size_t i = 0; i < T.size(); i++)
        std::cout << i << ": status " << r.status[i] << ", Rho " << r.Rho[i] << "\n";   // 0, 2 (OutOfRange, NaN), 0
    std::cout << r.failed_message.size() << " failed point(s)\n";
}

The vector forms of UpdateState_TPX/UpdateState_HPX evaluate the same points but throw at the first failure. With isMeshGrid = true they evaluate every combination of the three vectors.

docs.title: Result fields
docs.text:
ThermodynamicProperties (and the vectors of ThermodynamicPropertiesVector):

Field Meaning T, p, X, H temperature [K], pressure [Pa], bulk salinity [kg/kg], bulk specific enthalpy [J/kg]; T is a result of H–p–X, H of T–p–X phase phase region, a PhaseRegion; phase_name(phase) gives its name (Phase region) Rho, H, Cp, Mu bulk density [kg/m³], enthalpy, heat capacity [J/(kg K)], viscosity [Pa s] S_l, S_v, S_h phase fractions: volume fractions for H₂O–NaCl; the vapour mass fraction (quality) for the water models X_l, X_v salinity of the liquid and the vapour [kg/kg] Rho_l, Rho_v, Rho_h; H_l, H_v, H_h; Cp_l, Cp_v, Cp_h; Mu_l, Mu_v properties of the liquid, vapour and halite phases dRhodT, dRhodP ∂ρ/∂T [kg/(m³ K)], ∂ρ/∂p [kg/(m³ Pa)]; with _l, _v for the phases IsothermalCompressibility, IsobaricExpansivity (1/ρ) ∂ρ/∂p [1/Pa], −(1/ρ) ∂ρ/∂T [1/K]; with _l, _v for the phases

In a single-phase state, the bulk fields are those of the phase; fields of an absent phase are 0.

Multiphase states follow the definitions on Model and limitations: Rho and H are bulk values; Cp is the "frozen" heat capacity without latent heat (0 in V+L+H); Mu is not a mixture viscosity (a placeholder 1 in V+L, V+H and L+H; use Mu_l and Mu_v); IsothermalCompressibility is the equilibrium derivative; IsobaricExpansivity, dRhodT and dRhodP are not computed (0).

Unavailable properties. A property that cannot be evaluated at an otherwise valid state is NaN while the others are valid: for example the IAPS-84 viscosity outside its validity range (above 3500 bar at more than 150 °C, among others), and brine viscosities that depend on it.

docs.title: Python guide
docs.text:
The Python package xthermo gives you the H₂O–NaCl equation of state of Driesner & Heinrich (2007) and Driesner (2007), pure water (IAPS-84, IAPWS-95) and pure NaCl. You evaluate states on NumPy arrays of any shape and draw phase diagrams and property maps with a few Matplotlib helpers.

import numpy as np
import xthermo
from xthermo import H2ONaCl

sw = H2ONaCl.cH2ONaCl("IAPS84")                         # H2O-NaCl with the IAPS-84 water backend

T = np.array([300.0, 400.0, 500.0]) + 273.15            # K
s = xthermo.tpx(sw, T, 250e5, 0.032)                    # p = 250 bar in Pa, X = 3.2 wt% NaCl in kg/kg
print(s.phase_name)                                     # ['Liquid' 'V+L' 'V+H']
print(s.Rho)                                            # bulk density, kg/m³
print(s.X_v)                                            # salinity of the vapour phase, kg/kg (0 where absent)

docs.title: The models
docs.text:
Module Class System xthermo.H2ONaCl cH2ONaCl("IAPS84"), cH2ONaCl("IAPWS95") H₂O–NaCl; the argument selects the water equation of state xthermo.H2O cIAPS84(), cIAPWS95() pure water xthermo.NaCl cNaCl("IAPS84") pure NaCl (solid, liquid, vapour)

The Driesner correlations were fitted with IAPS-84, so "IAPS84" is the reference backend for H₂O–NaCl. "IAPWS95" gives slightly different brine properties; see Model and limitations.

Create a model once and reuse it for all your evaluations. A model object is not meant to be shared between threads; use one per thread.
